## What is a folder (a.k.a. directory)?

- A **folder** and a **directory** are the same thing, two names for one idea.
  - "Folder" is the word the graphical file browser uses.
  - "Directory" is the word the command line uses.
- A directory is a **container** that holds files and other directories.
- Directories form a **tree**: one top ("root"), branches, and leaves (files).

## The tree metaphor

```
/                          <- root of the whole file system (Linux/Mac)
├── home/
│   └── steve/
│       ├── Documents/
│       │   └── grant.docx
│       └── github/
│           └── workshops2026aug/
│               └── gentle-on-ramp/
│                   └── folders_and_navigation.qmd
└── tmp/
```

- On **Windows**, each drive has its own root: `C:\`, `D:\`, ...
- On **Mac/Linux**, there is one root `/`, and drives get mounted into it.

## Paths: how you name a location

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"} 
A **path** is a sequence of directory names that points to a file or folder.

- **Absolute path** — starts at the root, works from anywhere.
  - Linux/Mac: `/home/steve/Documents/grant.docx`
  - Windows: `C:\Users\steve\Documents\grant.docx`
- **Relative path** — starts from wherever you *currently are*.
  - `Documents/grant.docx` (if you are in `/home/steve`)
  - `../github/` (go up one level, then into `github`)

Two special names every directory has:

- `.` means "this directory"
- `..` means "the parent directory (one level up)"
:::

## Slashes: `/` vs `\`

- Linux and Mac use forward slash: `/home/steve/Documents`
- Windows uses backslash: `C:\Users\steve\Documents`
- Most modern Windows tools also accept forward slashes.
- In R and Python code, **always use forward slashes** even on Windows,
  or use `file.path()` / `os.path.join()` so your code is portable.

## Your home directory

Every user has a **home directory**, their personal top-level folder.

| System   | Typical location            | Shortcut |
|----------|-----------------------------|----------|
| Linux    | `/home/steve`               | `~`      |
| Mac      | `/Users/steve`              | `~`      |
| Windows  | `C:\Users\steve`            | `%USERPROFILE%` |

In a shell, `~` expands to your home. So `~/Documents` means
`/home/steve/Documents` for me, and `/Users/alice/Documents` for someone else.

# Three ways to navigate

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"} 
## 1. A graphical file browser (Nautilus, Finder, Explorer)

- **Linux (GNOME):** Nautilus, called "Files".
- **Mac:** Finder.
- **Windows:** File Explorer.

What they all give you:

- Double-click a folder to enter it.
- A **back** button and an **up** arrow to go to the parent.
- An **address bar** you can click to type a path.
- Drag-and-drop to move or copy files.
- Various right click commands and keyboard shortcuts.

Good for: browsing, quick one-off moves, previewing images/PDFs.
:::

## 2. A file-tree browser (in your editor)

Most editors show the folder tree in a sidebar.

- **VS Code / Positron / Cursor:** the "Explorer" panel on the left.
- **JupyterLab:** the file browser on the left.

Advantages over a general file browser:

- Click a file, it opens in the editor immediately.
- The tree reflects the **project root** you opened, so paths line up with your code.
- Right-click gives you "Reveal in Finder / Explorer", "Copy path",
  "Copy relative path", "Open in integrated terminal".

## 3. The command line (terminal)

Where to find it:

- **Linux:** GNOME Terminal, Konsole, or press `Ctrl` + `Alt` + `T`.
- **Mac:** Terminal.app, or iTerm2.
- **Windows:** PowerShell, Windows Terminal, or the old `cmd.exe`.

Inside your editor:

- VS Code / Positron: `` Ctrl + ` `` opens an integrated terminal.
- RStudio: the "Terminal" tab, next to "Console".

## Hidden files

Files whose names start with a dot (`.bashrc`, `.git/`) are **hidden** by default
on Linux and Mac. That is a convention, not a security feature. 
Windows has other conventions for hiding "system files"


# Command-line basics

## The four commands you use every minute

```bash
pwd                 # "print working directory": where am I?
ls                  # list files in the current directory
cd some/folder      # change directory into some/folder
cd ..               # go up one level
```

On Windows `cmd.exe` the equivalents are:

```bat
cd                  :: with no argument, prints the current directory
dir                 :: list files
cd some\folder      :: change directory
cd ..               :: go up one level
```

PowerShell accepts `pwd`, `ls`, and `cd` as aliases, so the bash commands above
work there too.

## `ls`: seeing what's in a directory

*Note the `-a` flag to see "hidden files" -- files with names 
that start with . (dot).


```bash
ls                  # names only
ls -l               # long form: permissions, size, date
ls -lh              # long form with human-readable sizes (1.2K, 3.4M)
ls -a               # include hidden files (dotfiles)
ls -la              # both
ls Documents        # list a specific directory without cd-ing in
```

Windows `cmd.exe`:

```bat
dir                 :: names, sizes, dates
dir /a              :: include hidden
dir /s              :: recurse into subfolders
```

## `cd`: moving around

```bash
cd                  # with no argument: go home (~)
cd ~                # same thing, explicitly
cd -                # go back to the previous directory you were in
cd /                # go to the root of the file system
cd ..               # up one
cd ../..            # up two
cd ~/github/workshops2026aug   # absolute path from home
```

Tab-completion is your friend: type `cd Doc` then press `Tab`, the shell
finishes `Documents/` if that's the only match, or shows options if not.

## Making, moving, and removing

```bash
mkdir new_folder            # make a directory
mkdir -p a/b/c              # make a chain of nested directories at once

cp file.txt backup.txt      # copy a file
cp -r folder/ backup/       # copy a folder and its contents (recursive)

mv old.txt new.txt          # rename
mv file.txt ~/Documents/    # move into another folder

rm file.txt                 # delete a file (no trash, gone immediately!)
rm -r folder/               # delete a folder and everything in it
```

**Warning:** `rm` does **not** send files to a trash / recycle bin. It deletes
them straight away. Be especially careful with `rm -r` and never with `sudo`
unless you are sure.

## A quick tour, live

```bash
pwd                                    # /home/steve
cd github/workshops2026aug             # into the workshop repo
pwd                                    # /home/steve/github/workshops2026aug
ls                                     # see what's here
cd gentle-on-ramp                      # into today's folder
ls -lh                                 # long listing with sizes
cd ..                                  # back up one level
cd ~                                   # back home
```

## Absolute vs. relative in practice

Suppose you are in `/home/steve/github/workshops2026aug/gentle-on-ramp/`
and you want to open `../r_graphics/Steve_Rozen_R_graphics_for_bioinformatics_2026_08_03.qmd`.

Both of these work:

```bash
# relative, shorter, breaks if you cd somewhere else first
xdg-open ../r_graphics/Steve_Rozen_R_graphics_for_bioinformatics_2026_08_03.qmd

# absolute, longer, works from anywhere
xdg-open /home/steve/github/workshops2026aug/r_graphics/Steve_Rozen_R_graphics_for_bioinformatics_2026_08_03.qmd
```

Relative paths are great inside a project (your scripts stay portable when the
project moves). Absolute paths are great in one-off commands.

## Getting from the file browser to the terminal (and back)

- **Nautilus:** right-click inside a folder → "Open in Terminal".
- **Finder (Mac):** drag a folder onto the Terminal icon, or enable
  "New Terminal at Folder" in System Settings → Keyboard → Services.
- **Explorer (Windows):** type `cmd` or `powershell` in the address bar and
  press Enter, the shell opens in that folder.
- Going the other way — from a shell to the file browser:
  - Linux: `xdg-open .`
  - Mac:   `open .`
  - Windows: `explorer .`

## Wildcards (globs)

The shell expands patterns before running the command.

```bash
ls *.qmd              # every .qmd file in this directory
ls slides/*.pptx      # every .pptx in the slides/ subdirectory
rm tmp_*.png          # every file starting with tmp_ and ending in .png
ls **/*.R             # every .R file at any depth (needs shopt -s globstar)
```

- `*` means "any string of characters, no slashes".
- `?` means "exactly one character".
- `[abc]` means "one of a, b, or c".

## Where am I in R and Python?

R:

```r
getwd()                           # current working directory
setwd("~/github/workshops2026aug") # change it
list.files()                      # like ls
```

Python:

```python
import os
os.getcwd()
os.chdir("/home/steve/github/workshops2026aug")
os.listdir()
```

In RStudio / Positron / Jupyter, when you open a **project**, the working
directory is set to the project root automatically. Use relative paths from
there and your code stays portable.

## Takeaways

- Folder = directory. One tree. Every location has a **path**.
- `~` is home. `.` is here. `..` is up one.
- Four commands cover 90% of navigation: `pwd`, `ls`, `cd`, and tab-completion.
- The file browser, the editor's file-tree, and the terminal are three views of
  the **same** filesystem, use whichever fits the task.
- `rm` has no undo. Measure twice, cut once.
